Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the basic elements of CT, including the information obtained during imaging and the
manner in which it is used to create a diagnostic image.
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of CT, including the advantages and
disadvantages of using CT compared with other imaging modalities.
Discuss common musculoskeletal indications for CT and the role of CT in the diagnosis and
management of various orthopaedic conditions.
Principles of CT
Basic Physics of CT
Fundamental components of a CT system include a gantry, table, and scanner console.
X-rays are generated using an x-ray tube that rotates relative to a detector.

The x-rays are absorbed, scattered, or propagated to a detector. The information is processed
to form a tomographic image.

Basic Physics of CT
Standard CT systems include a gantry, a table, and a separate console (Resource 1). The
technologist uses the console to set the parameters of the study and then advances the
patient into the circular frame, also known as the gantry. X-rays generated in the gantry
are propagated through the patient to an array of detectors (detector array). Data
collected from the detectors are used to create individual thin, cross-sectional
(tomographic) images that are then sequentially combined to form an axial CT series.
The images are displayed using different shades of gray. The brightness or darkness of
each image is determined by how much of the x-ray beam is blocked by the patient
(attenuation). Attenuation can be quantified and is expressed in Hounsfield units. For
materials with high attenuation, such as bone or metal, most of the emitted x-rays that
enter the patient fail to reach the detector array. The opposite is true for low-attenuating
materials, such as air, water, or fat. Hounsfield units range from −1,000 for air, to 0 for
water, to 1,000+ for dense materials such as bone.1
Radiation Dose
CT radiation dose generally is higher than that of equivalent radiographs.
Calculating the radiation dose for CT is complicated. The dose may vary considerably between
patients or even within the same patient.
The dose is related to the length of the segment of a patient that is scanned.

Radiation Dose

Radiation is a crucial consideration in selecting any imaging study. Determination of an
effective dose for a given CT scan is complicated; may change with subtle variations in
the protocol; and is affected by various factors, including patient size and positioning.
Providing specific information regarding the clinical indication for CT when ordering the
study will ultimately optimize the imaging study and limit unnecessary radiation.
Because the dose is related to how much of the patient is scanned, a follow-up study of
the L5 pars interarticularis, for example, should include just that region rather than the
entire lumbar spine.
Image Reconstruction and Optimization
Axial tomographic images can be reconstructed into any plane, even curved planes. Three
orthogonal planes are most commonly created.
Axial images also can be used to create three-dimensional (3D) images and for 3D printing.

Image Reconstruction and Optimization
Initial axial tomographic images are reconstructed into coronal and sagittal images that
are perpendicular to the original images. The CT technologist generally creates these
images immediately after the examination. In certain clinical scenarios, reconstruction
images in additional planes are added. For example, in patients with recurrent
glenohumeral instability and secondary glenoid bone loss, volume-rendered 3D images
of the scapula and humerus may aid evaluation of glenoid version, glenoid bone stock,
and humeral subluxation2,3 (Figure 1; Resources 2 and 3). Some picture archiving and
communication systems allow the reader to make reconstruction images.

Figure 1 Images of the right shoulder of a 33-year-old man with recurrent right anterior
glenohumeral dislocations. A, Grashey radiograph demonstrates a small Hill-Sachs
lesion (solid arrow) and subtle density projecting inferior and medial to the
glenohumeral joint (dashed arrow). Sagittal (B) and axial (C) CT scans obtained
perpendicular to the glenoid show a flattened anterior glenoid (arrowheads; B) and
flattening of the superolateral humeral head (arrow; C). Three-dimensional CT
reconstruction images show the shoulder (D) and separation of the scapula (E) and the
humeral head (F), which enables improved visualization of the small osseous Bankart
and Hill-Sachs lesions. In panel E, the arrowheads indicate the flattened glenoid, and the
arrow indicates the osseous Bankart lesion. In panel F, the arrow indicates the Hill-Sachs
lesion. (Courtesy of Kevin McGill, MD, MPH, San Francisco, CA.)
Advantages of CT
Image Formation
CT scanners are fast and readily available.
The tomographic nature of the images facilitates detailed anatomic evaluation and
manipulation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:45 AM
AAOS | Computed Tomography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003005
4/24

CT can be used in image-guided procedures, such as biopsies, ablations, and injections.
CT has higher contrast resolution than radiography and a higher spatial resolution than MRI.

Image Formation
Modern CT scanners are fast, performing most scans in less than 1 minute. They are
available in most hospitals, many emergency departments, and some outpatient centers.
Although CT and MRI function on completely different scientific principles, the
tomographic nature of the images facilitates comparison of diagnostic images. Nuclear
medicine imaging, such as positron emission tomography, frequently is performed in
combination with CT to create fused positron emission tomography/CT images that
provide anatomic and functional data. Standardization of the imaging planes also is
convenient in planning and performing interventional procedures.
Spatial resolution, the ability to distinguish between objects of different density that are
near one another, is superior with CT compared with MRI. This property of CT allows for
visualization of osseous detail, facilitating characterization of complex comminuted
fractures and nondisplaced small bone (eg, midfoot) fractures. Modern CT scanners
acquire initial data as thin (≤1 mm) sections, which may be used for evaluation of
nondisplaced fractures or reconstructed into thicker (≥2 mm) sections that contain fewer
images with less noise than thinner sections, facilitating rapid interpretation.
Image Modification
Windowing is a useful tool for evaluating different organ systems on the same CT scan.

Image Modification

CT grayscale images can be manipulated to optimize visualization of certain pathology
via a process known as windowing in which the viewer can adjust the CT values that are
displayed1,4 (Resources 4 and 5; Figure 2).
Figure 2 Axial CT scans of the chest of a 63-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell
carcinoma obtained through four different CT windows: bone (A), lungs (B), angiography
(C; useful for detection of pulmonary emboli), and soft tissue (D). The CT scans show
cortical destruction of the inner cortex of the right posterior rib (closed arrowhead in
panel A), pathologic rib fracture (solid arrow in panel A), emphysema (dashed arrow in
panel B), contrast material in the aorta (star in panel C), and a soft-tissue mass (open
arrowhead in panel D). (Courtesy of Kevin McGill, MD, MPH, San Francisco, CA.)
Nondiagnostic Features
No absolute contraindications to a non–contrast examination exist.
Scanner diameters for most CT systems are larger than those for MRI, which allows for
imaging of patients who are larger.
CT has shorter acquisition times than MRI, which enhances its usefulness for trauma and
pediatric examinations.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:45 AM
AAOS | Computed Tomography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003005
6/24

The speed of image acquisition facilitates use in interventional procedures, especially if using
CT fluoroscopy.

Nondiagnostic Features
Few relative contraindications (eg, pregnancy) and no absolute contraindications to non–
contrast CT exist. MRI, is associated with many relative and absolute contraindications,
especially in patients with certain implanted devices.
The larger scanner diameter and decreased scan time make CT preferable in patients
who are larger or claustrophobic. This speed can be leveraged to enhance the ease of
interventional procedures by using continuous and intermittent versions of CT
fluoroscopy. In standard continuous CT fluoroscopy, reconstruction images of
continuously acquired data are used to guide needle placement in real time during
interventional procedures. Alternatively, an intermittent scan mode, in which the
operator is able to acquire discrete axial images at any time by stepping on a pedal, can
be used. This method may be referred to as step and shoot5 (Resource 6). Compared
with the traditional method of performing CT, which involves repeatedly obtaining
truncated low-dose CT scans during the procedure, CT fluoroscopy may decrease
procedure time and radiation dose to the patient.
Disadvantages of CT
Image Formation
Metal artifact may limit evaluation in patients postoperatively.
MRI soft-tissue contrast is much greater than that of CT.

Image Formation

Metal artifact is a widespread problem, especially in postoperative imaging, and it
may limit evaluation of soft-tissue pathology adjacent to implanted hardware. Metal
artifact also is a considerable problem in patients with external fixation and patients
with multiple bullet fragments. Multiple techniques to decrease metal artifact have
been developed and include adjusting the scanning parameters, manipulating the
data used to produce an image, and obtaining additional information during the scan6
(Resource 7).
CT has better spatial resolution than MRI but less than that of ultrasonography.
Ultrasonography, dissimilar from CT and MRI, is less affected by metal artifact and,
therefore, may be useful in evaluating soft-tissue pathology adjacent to implanted
hardware7 (Resource 8). MRI is associated with superior soft-tissue contrast
resolution compared with CT, which makes it ideal for identifying soft-tissue
abnormalities and assessing bone marrow.
Image Modification
The quality of reconstructed CT images depends on the quality of the initial acquisition.

Image Modification
CT scans usually are obtained in the axial plane and then reconstructed via various
methods. If the initial data are suboptimal (eg, motion artifact), the reconstructed
images will be poorer. Therefore, CT occasionally must be repeated multiple times to
obtain diagnostic images, increasing radiation dose to the patient.
Nondiagnostic Features
CT is impractical in patients with extreme morbid obesity.
Allergic reactions to CT contrast are more common compared with MRI contrast; however,
contrast rarely is used for musculoskeletal indications (except arthrography and myelography).
CT rarely is indicated in pregnant patients.

CT should be limited in pediatric patients.
Use of intravenous contrast should be limited in patients with renal failure.

Nondiagnostic Features
CT is impractical in patients with extreme morbid obesity because of limitations on
the aperture size and table weight. Traditional CT systems have an aperture size of 60
to 70 cm and a maximum table weight of 400 to 450 lb. Certain specialized systems
for routine diagnostic scanning may have apertures as large as 85 cm and the ability
to accommodate patients who weigh as much as 680 lb8 (Resource 9). The radiation
dose to patients with extreme morbid obesity (body mass index ≥50 kg/m2) is
substantially higher than that to a smaller patient undergoing the same study.
Because the patient is closer to the limits of the system, scan quality decreases.
Surgeons should discuss such patients with the radiologist and/or radiation
technologist before ordering CT to identify potential options to avoid unnecessary
radiation and delays in patient care.
Allergic reactions to contrast are another concern for some CT studies. Although
uncommonly required for musculoskeletal studies, contrast can be administered via
intra-articular, intrathecal, and intravenous routes. However, modern iodinated
contrast used for CT studies is associated with a higher rate of allergic reactions
compared with modern gadolinium-based contrast used for MRI (iodinated, 0.6%;
gadolinium, 0.01% to 0.22%). Even patients without allergies may experience mild
symptoms during the injections9 (Resource 10). If a patient reports a prior adverse
reaction to iodinated contrast, then a detailed account of the symptoms should be
elicited before ordering CT to determine the appropriate premedication regimen,
which may take as long as 13 hours.
CT is rarely indicated in pregnant patients. If CT is being considered in a pregnant
patient, the risk and advantages to the patient and the potential adverse effects to the
fetus from ionizing radiation should be considered10 (Resource 11). Some situations
in which contrast-enhanced CT may be reasonable in pregnant patients include acute
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:45 AM
AAOS | Computed Tomography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003005
9/24

trauma, in which a high suspicion for acute vascular injury and pulmonary embolism
exists; this is a leading preventable cause of maternal death11 (Resource 12).
Although CT should be limited in pediatric patients, pediatric CT protocols involve the
use of less radiation than adult CT protocols. The Radiological Society of North
America is a reliable source for identifying the approximate amount of radiation used
in CT12 (Resource 13).
Although contrast is not contraindicated in patients with renal failure, the addition of
iodinated contrast should be considered carefully because of the minor risk of
contrast-induced nephropathy, which is rare.9 Results from recent studies suggest
that the previously reported relationship between intravenous contrast and post-
contrast kidney injury may be more correlative than causative13 (Resource 14).
Musculoskeletal Indications
Trauma and Sports
CT may be used for confirmation of subtle fractures, characterization of complex fractures,
and assessment of bone healing.
3D CT reconstruction images or multiplanar images aid in treatment planning.
CT arthrography may be performed if a patient is unable to undergo MRI.
Knee menisci, ligaments, and articular cartilage
Hip labrum and articular cartilage
Shoulder labrum and articular cartilage but limited for rotator cuff

Trauma and Sports
Although comminuted displaced fractures can be identified easily on radiographs, more
subtle fractures may require CT for confirmation. CT also is useful to assess more
complex fractures that may be difficult to evaluate precisely on radiographs because of
osseous structure overlap. Software can be used to create and manipulate 3D CT
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:45 AM
AAOS | Computed Tomography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003005
10/24

reconstruction images and multiplanar reformatted images. Multiplanar reformatted
images commonly are used in the trauma setting for preoperative planning. This
technique may be especially helpful in the classification of complex fractures (Resource
15) and in virtual fracture reduction (Resource 16), both of which may occur in multiple
planes. However, 3D and multiplanar reformatted images require adequate baseline
images to be useful.14,15 After high-energy trauma, contrast-enhanced CT may
accelerate the diagnosis and subsequent management of vascular injuries via surgical or
interventional techniques. These images are particularly useful for quantification of bone
loss in patients with shoulder instability.3
In CT arthrography, intra-articular contrast is added to enhance visualization of intra-
articular structures (Figure 3). This technique can be used in patients in whom MRI
and/or gadolinium is contraindicated.
Increased use of cone-beam CT has been observed in orthopaedic offices. Some of the
advantages include low cost, less radiation, increased spatial resolution, and the ability
to image a patient bearing weight. Some of the disadvantages compared with standard
multidetector CT are limited field of view, increased motion artifact, and limited
evaluation of soft-tissue pathology16 (Resource 17).
3D C-arm is a relatively new technology in which digital volume tomography is used to
create a 3D data set using two-dimensional fluoroscopic images. These images, which
can be generated intraoperatively, are used in various settings, including fracture
reduction and internal fixation, hardware evaluation, and verification and management
of coalitions. Some 3D C-arms also contain a convenient digital interface, enabling
intraoperative communication with navigation systems17 (Resource 18).

Figure 3 Images of the right shoulder of a 59-year-old man who has new shoulder pain
and a history of shoulder surgery. A, AP radiograph demonstrates three screws in the
glenoid. Coronal (B) and sagittal (C) CT arthrograms show multiple loose bodies in the
subcoracoid bursa (arrowheads; B) and contrast material in the subacromial subdeltoid
bursa (arrow; C), which is consistent with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear. D, Sagittal CT
arthrogram shows contrast material surrounding two of the malpositioned glenoid
screws (dashed arrow) that extend into the glenohumeral joint. (Courtesy of Kevin
McGill, MD, MPH, San Francisco, CA.)
Tumor, Infection, and Inflammation
CT may be helpful for characterization of suspected neoplastic and other lesions, especially
those involving bone or soft-tissue mineralization. Interventional procedures, such as bone
biopsy, sclerotherapy, and radiofrequency ablation often are performed under CT guidance.
SEND FEEDBACK

CT may be used to identify soft-tissue abscesses or necrotizing fasciitis in patients in whom
infection is suspected.
Dual-energy CT has various uses, including its most common musculoskeletal application,
which is in evaluation of crystalline arthropathy, such as gout.

Tumor, Infection, and Inflammation
Occasionally, CT is used for characterization of suspected neoplastic lesions. CT is helpful
in the evaluation of calcifications, cortical involvement, and pathologic fractures. CT also
is beneficial for certain nonmalignant lesions, such as osteoid osteomas and myositis
ossificans (Figure 4). Although MRI is still the preferred imaging modality, full-body low-
dose CT is an efficient, cost-effective option for evaluating multiple myeloma18 (Figure
5).

Figure 5 Coronal (A) and sagittal (B) reformatted full-body low-dose CT scans of a 55-
year-old man with low back pain, anemia, and a clonal bone marrow plasma cell
percentage of 21% show several osteolytic lesions (arrows) in the axial skeleton,

CT is especially helpful in identifying bone involvement and cortical breakthrough of
suspicious lesions. CT is the optimal imaging modality for performing bone-related
interventions, such as bone biopsies, sclerotherapy of aneurysmal bone cysts, and
radiofrequency ablation of osteoid osteomas. Identifying deep fluid collections and
draining abscesses are facilitated by CT. If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected, CT is an ideal
imaging modality because of its ability to scan a large section of the body quickly and
identify gas in the soft tissues easily.

Dual-energy CT is a technique in which two x-ray energy spectra are used in one CT scan.
This technique takes advantage of the different properties of structures imaged at
different energy levels. Dual-energy CT can provide information about tissue
composition, while also improving metal artifact reduction and image optimization.6
Dual-energy CT is useful in patients in whom gout is suspected to distinguish between
gout and calcific mineralization and in patients with known gout in whom volumetric
analysis of tophi is useful for guiding treatment19 (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Images show acute tophaceous gout. Images of the toes of a46-year-old man
with a normal serum uric acid level in whom The patient developed an acute episode of
gout occurred despite having taken the prescribed medications. A, PA radiograph
demonstrates vague mineralization surrounding the first metatarsophalangeal joint and
the second proximal interphalangeal joint. B, Plantar, three-dimensional dual-energy CT
reconstruction image shows the mineralization, which corresponds with the urate
deposits (green areas) and is consistent with classic tophaceous gouty arthritis. Images
of the second digit of a 62-year-old man with swelling and pain around the digit.
Although the patient had a remote history of gout, his serum uric acid level was normal.
C, Sagittal CT image shows that the second digit flexor tendon is thickened, contains
mineralization, and is surrounded by inflammatory changes. D, Sagittal, color-coded,
dual-energy CT scan shows green urate crystal deposits along the flexor tendon, which is
consistent with gout-related tendinopathy. (Reproduced with permission from Desai MA,
Peterson JJ, Garner HW, Kransdorf MJ: Clinical utility of dual-energy CT for evaluation of
tophaceous gout. Radiographics 2011;31[5]:1365-1377.)

Arthroplasty
CT is useful for surgical navigation guidance during arthroplasty and the creation of prostheses
and models.
CT may indicate hardware complications, and periprosthetic fractures and ceramic fractures
can be identified via CT.

Arthroplasty
Metal artifact reduction techniques (including dual-energy CT) have improved the quality
of CT, making it an excellent imaging modality for evaluation of periprosthetic fractures;
however, before the initial surgical procedure, CT scans can be used to assess leg-length
discrepancies or for preoperative templating of prior robot-assisted procedures. For
revision arthroplasty, conventional CT may help create custom prostheses and assess
preoperative bone stock and bone alignment. CT also is useful for evaluating the
position of hardware (Figure 7) and detecting failed nonmetal components, such as
fracture or fragmentation of ceramic or polyethylene liners.

Figure 7 Images of the left hip of a patient with persistent anterior groin pain after
noncemented total hip arthroplasty. AP (A) and cross-table lateral (B) radiographs
demonstrate no radiographic evidence of retroversion. Axial (C) and sagittal (D) CT scans
show a noncemented acetabular implant with a prominent anterior rim. AP (E) and
cross-table lateral (F) radiographs obtained after acetabular revision to manage iliopsoas
impingement. (Copyright Rafael J. Sierra, MD, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN.)
Spine
CT is a valuable tool for the initial evaluation of spinal trauma.
CT is useful to evaluate for disk disease and other degenerative processes if MRI is not readily
available.
Complex scoliotic curvatures and potential hardware complications after spinal fusion can be
evaluated via CT. Postoperative evaluation can be performed for fusion, fractures, and
hardware failure.
CT myelography may be an alternative to MRI for evaluating spinal canal pathology in certain
patients.
CT also may afford better evaluation of mineralization, such as facet and vertebral body
osteophytes or ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, as an adjunct to MRI
preoperatively.


Spine
CT is the first imaging modality for evaluating spinal trauma, especially complex
fractures. It also is useful for evaluating degenerative arthropathy, destructive osseous
lesions, and postoperative fusion20 (Resource 19). CT also may aid in evaluating complex
scoliotic curvature and spinal fusion hardware.
Myelography, imaging after contrast is injected into the subarachnoid space, is no longer
performed without subsequent CT. CT myelography can be used for problem solving if
MRI does not provide adequate information. Nonmyelographic CT may be performed
preoperatively to evaluate osteophytes and bony anatomy21 (Figure 8). CT can be used
to facilitate computer-navigated surgery.
